title: Reengineering the Corporation
author: Michael Hammer and James Champy
theme: Companies achieve dramatic gains not by tweaking old tasks but by starting over and redesigning whole business processes around the customer.
summary: Michael Hammer and James Champy argue that most large companies were built for a world that no longer exists. Their structures grew from the industrial idea of splitting work into small, specialised tasks, each handled by a different department. That design worked when markets were stable, but it produces slow handoffs, errors, duplicated checks and layers of managers whose main job is to stitch the fragments back together.

Three forces, they say, have made this model obsolete: customers who now expect more and can choose freely, competition that has become global and intense, and change that has become constant. Incremental improvement cannot close the gap. Instead, firms must reengineer, which the authors define as fundamentally rethinking and radically redesigning business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in cost, quality, service and speed.

The key shift is to stop looking at departments and start looking at processes: the complete chain of activities that turns inputs into something a customer values, such as filling an order or developing a product. The book's cases, including credit approvals at IBM and supplier payments at Ford, show how removing needless steps and handoffs cut cycle times and costs sharply.

Redesigned processes tend to share features. Several jobs are combined into one, workers make decisions themselves, steps happen in a natural order, checks and reconciliations are reduced, and a single case manager can serve as the customer's point of contact.

These changes ripple outward. Departments give way to process teams, narrow tasks become broader jobs, controlled employees become empowered ones, pay shifts towards results, and managers move from supervising to coaching. Information technology is treated as an enabler that lets companies break old rules, not as a way to automate existing waste.
Finally, the authors stress that reengineering must be led from the top, with clear owners for each process, because it is disruptive and often fails when attempted halfway.
takeaway: Don't automate or patch a broken process; ask why it exists and redesign it from scratch around the outcome the customer needs.

questions.q: How do Hammer and Champy define reengineering?
options: Gradual, continuous improvement of existing tasks
Fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes for dramatic improvement
Cutting headcount across all departments by a fixed percentage
Installing new computer systems on top of current workflows
questions.why: The book defines reengineering as fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of processes to achieve dramatic gains in cost, quality, service and speed.

questions.q: What is the main unit of analysis the authors want managers to focus on?
questions.why: They argue companies should be organised and improved around end-to-end processes rather than departments or tasks.

questions.q: Which three forces do the authors say have made the old organisational model obsolete?
questions.why: The book highlights more demanding customers, intensified competition and constant change as the forces driving the need for reengineering.

questions.q: What older idea do the authors blame for fragmented, inefficient corporate structures?
options: The division of labour into small specialised tasks
questions.why: They trace the problem to the industrial-era principle of breaking work into narrow tasks spread across many departments.

questions.q: According to the book, what is a business process?
options: A set of activities that takes inputs and creates an output of value to the customer
A software application used by employees
questions.why: A process is the complete chain of activities that turns inputs into a result the customer values.

questions.q: What role does information technology play in reengineering, according to the authors?
options: It should automate existing steps to make them faster
It is irrelevant to process redesign
It enables new ways of working that break old rules
It should be introduced only after reengineering is finished
questions.why: The authors see IT as an enabler of radically new processes, warning against simply automating existing waste.

questions.q: Which feature is common in reengineered processes?
options: More approval layers to reduce risk
Several jobs combined into one, with workers making decisions
Each step handled by a separate specialist
questions.why: Redesigned processes typically compress jobs and push decision-making to the people doing the work.

questions.q: How does the role of managers change in a reengineered organisation?
options: They shift from supervising to coaching
questions.why: With empowered process teams, managers move from controlling work to coaching and supporting people.

questions.q: Why do the authors reject incremental improvement as the answer?
options: It is too expensive to measure
It cannot deliver the dramatic gains needed when the underlying design is broken
Employees resist small changes more than large ones
questions.why: They argue small tweaks to a fundamentally flawed process cannot close the large performance gap companies face.

questions.q: Who must lead a reengineering effort, according to the book?
options: Senior leadership, with clear owners for each process
questions.why: Because reengineering is disruptive and cross-functional, the authors insist it be driven from the top with designated process owners.
